CVE-2026-62313.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-62313.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 7.3.0, project-level enforcement of `restricted.containers.privilege=isolated` can be trivially bypassed, allowing a user to create a non-isolated (shared host idmap) container in a project that is configured to forbid them. The restriction only rejects an explicitly set `security.idmap.isolated=false` (or empty) and fails to enforce anything when the key is omitted entirely. Because an unset `security.idmap.isolated` defaults to `false` (non-isolation), a user simply leaves the key out and obtains exactly the container state the restriction is meant to forbid. This defeats the tenant-isolation guarantee the restriction exists to provide. Containers in the project share the host uid/gid map instead of receiving unique, non-overlapping ranges, weakening the isolation boundary between co-tenant containers and the host. Version 7.3.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-81496.title: Arbitrary file write on host via path traversal in instance backup import
CVE-2026-81496.description: ## Summary `POST /1.0/instances` with an `application/octet-stream` body (instance backup import) reads the instance name from the tarball's `backup/index.yaml` verbatim and uses it as an on-disk path segment. A project user with the `can_create_instances` entitlement can set `name: ../../../../etc/cron.d/x`, causing the root Incus daemon to create a directory and unpack attacker-controlled tarball content outside the storage pool - before any name validation runs. This yields arbitrary directory creation and arbitrary-content file write as root, and thus host RCE. ## Root Cause In `createFromBackup` (`cmd/incusd/instances_post.go`), the tarball metadata is parsed by `backup.GetInfo` (`internal/server/backup/backup_info.go:64-160`), which loads `result.Name` straight from `index.yaml` via YAML unmarshal with NO validation - no `filepath.Clean`, no `IsAPIName`, no `/` or `..` rejection. The name then flows to `pool.CreateInstanceFromBackup` -> `project.Instance(srcBackup.Project, srcBackup.Name)` (`internal/server/storage/backend.go:744`) -> `vol.MountPath()` -> `GetVolumeMountPath` = `VarPath('storage-pools', pool, 'containers', <name>)` -> `EnsureMountPath` `os.Mkdir` + `CreateVolumeFromBackup` content unpack. `instance.ValidName` exists only at `instances_post.go:1452`, which is on the JSON-dispatch path and is never reached for the octet-stream branch (dispatch returns at `:1157`). ## Impact Root-owned arbitrary directory creation and arbitrary-content file write outside the storage pool (e.g. `/etc/cron.d/`), leading to host remote code execution. Snapshot names (`bInfo.Snapshots[]`) are a second identical vector. ## Proof of Concept 1. Build an instance backup tarball whose `backup/index.yaml` sets `name: ../../../../etc/cron.d/pwn` and whose `container/rootfs` contains a crafted cron file body. 2. `curl -X POST --data-binary @backup.tar -H 'Content-Type: application/octet-stream' https://incus/1.0/instances` (as a user with `can_create_instances`). 3. The daemon writes attacker content to `/etc/cron.d/pwn` as root. ## Attack Chain 1. Entry: `POST /1.0/instances`, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, no `X-Incus-name`. Guard: none for this branch -> `createFromBackup` (`instances_post.go:1157`). 2. Parse: `bInfo, _ := backup.GetInfo(backupFile, ...)` (`instances_post.go:851`) reads `Name` from `index.yaml`. Guard: `GetInfo` (`backup_info.go:64-160`) - none. Bypass proof: field returned untouched from YAML unmarshal; no `Clean`/`IsAPIName`/`..` check in the function (verified at HEAD). 3. Restriction check: `AllowInstanceCreation` (`instances_post.go:871`) validates project restrictions only, not name syntax. Passes. 4. Sink: `pool.CreateInstanceFromBackup(*bInfo, ...)` (`instances_post.go:992`) -> `project.Instance(proj, bInfo.Name)` (`backend.go:744`) -> `vol.MountPath()` -> `EnsureMountPath` `os.Mkdir` (`internal/server/storage/drivers/volume.go`) + content unpack, as root, BEFORE `internalImportFromBackup` and BEFORE the unreachable `ValidName` at `:1452`. 5. Impact: root arbitrary dir create + attacker-content file write -> host RCE. ## Bypass Evidence No guard exists between the tarball name and the disk write. Go's `filepath.Join` collapses `..`: `filepath.Join('/var/lib/incus/storage-pools/p/containers','../../../../etc/cron.d/x')` = `/var/lib/etc/cron.d/x` (verified by running it; deeper `..` reaches `/etc/cron.d/x`). Same class as CVE-2026-48753 but a distinct, unfixed entry point (record name used as path segment, not a symlink inside the archive payload). ## Affected Versions `<= 7.2.0` (vulnerable code verified present on latest release tag v7.2.0 and on HEAD 60d85b3e; no fix commit on `cmd/incusd/instances_post.go` between v7.2.0 and HEAD). ## Suggested Fix Apply `instance.ValidName(bInfo.Name, false)` (and validate each snapshot name) immediately after `backup.GetInfo`, before any storage I/O. ## Credit Vulnerability independently discovered and responsibly disclosed by Zhixi 'Jace' Sun (@manus-use).

CVE-2026-81501.title: Restricted client can import a private image from another project
CVE-2026-81501.description: ### Summary A project-restricted TLS client that cannot `GET /1.0/images/{fingerprint}` for a **private** image in another project can still import that same fingerprint into their own project. `imageDownload` reuses any matching local image via `GetImageFromAnyProject` without checking `Public` or `CanView`. Image blobs are stored globally under `var/images/<fingerprint>`, so the caller receives the private image properties and files. This is the image-object counterpart of GHSA-c9f5-j9c3-mhrg (instance copy from `req.Source.Project` without `CanView`). It is not a privileged-container escape. ### Affected - Runtime reproduction: Ubuntu 24.04 package **Incus 6.0.0** (`6.0.0-1ubuntu0.3`) in an isolated Docker environment. - Same unguarded call is present on `lxc/incus` at `v7.3.0-432-gf216a6d46` in `cmd/incusd/daemon_images.go`. - Full release range should be confirmed by maintainers. ### Contrast (same restricted client, same fingerprint) | Request | Result | | --- | --- | | `GET /1.0/images/<fp>?project=default` | **404** (`imageGet` requires `CanView` or public/secret) | | `POST /1.0/images?project=hunt-b` with `source.type=image` pulling from an attacker HTTPS server that only echoes `<fp>` | operation **Success**; image now listed in `hunt-b` with the victim `properties` | The attacker server never supplies image bytes. Incus clones the local private record and files. A harmless marker (`INCUS-HUNT-MARKER`) in the victim image properties appears in the attacker project. ### Impact A restricted client with `CanCreateImages` (or the ability to create an instance from an image) in their own project, who already knows a private image fingerprint from another project, can: - copy that image's properties and global blob into their project; - then view, export, or launch instances from it inside their project. This breaks Incus project isolation for private images. **Limitation:** the 64-hex fingerprint is not returned by `GET` / list to a caller without `CanView`. The attacker must obtain it out of band (logs, backups, a former project membership, a predictable custom image, etc.). No victim interaction is required after that. ### Root cause `imageGet` / `imagesGet` / `imageExport` apply `CheckPermission(ObjectImage, CanView)` and hide private images behind 404. `imageDownload`, after a dest-project miss, does: ```go _, imgInfo, err = tx.GetImageFromAnyProject(ctx, fp) // then CreateImage into the caller project — no Public / CanView check ``` Reachable from: - `POST /1.0/images` with `source.type=image` - `POST /1.0/instances` when `source.server != ''` `AllowImageDownload` only enforces `restricted.images.servers` (remote host allowlist). It is not an object-level `CanView` check. ### Suggested fix After `GetImageFromAnyProject` succeeds, only reuse the local image if: 1. `imgInfo.Public` is true, or 2. `CheckPermission` on `ObjectImage(imgInfo.Project, fingerprint)` with `EntitlementCanView` succeeds. Otherwise continue with a real remote download. Do not copy the private local image. ### Dedup Not a duplicate of: - GHSA-mq9x-prm8-3vpw / GHSA-c9f5-j9c3-mhrg — instance copy `Source.Project` without `CanView` (same class, different object and entry point) - GHSA-p8mm-23gg-jc9r — simplestreams concatenated fingerprint - GHSA-f6m5-xw2g-xc4x / GHSA-p2v3-6wvc-cv3p — fingerprint used as a filesystem path - GHSA-8gw4-p4wq-4hcv — URL import HEAD SSRF - Incus 7.3 leftover name-as-path / OpenRoot issues ### PoC Isolated Docker environment attached as `incus-private-image-anyproject.zip`. ```bash unzip incus-private-image-anyproject.zip cd incus-private-image-anyproject ./run.sh ``` Expected: `all_checks_passed: true`, `verdict=private_image_cross_project_reuse_reproduced_at_runtime`. The container starts Ubuntu 24.04 + distro Incus 6.0.0, creates a private image in `default` (marker in `properties.description`), a project `hunt-b`, and a restricted TLS cert bound only to `hunt-b`. It then runs the contrast above. Harmless marker only; no instance is launched. `results/runtime.json` from our run is included. ### Severity Medium. Suggested: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` = 6.3. | Metric | Value | Reason | | --- | --- | --- | | AV | N | HTTPS API | | AC | H | 64-hex fingerprint required; not enumerable via GET/list (404) | | PR | L | project-restricted TLS client with image-create rights, not admin | | UI | N | no victim interaction | | S | C | breaks project isolation (same Scope as GHSA-c9f5) | | C | H | full private image (properties + rootfs blob) | | I | N | victim image is not modified | | A | N | no availability impact | If maintainers treat fingerprint knowledge like instance-name knowledge in GHSA-c9f5, the matching vector is `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` = 7.7. I am reporting 6.3. ### Credit Yuliang Xiao

GHSA-443p-7392-h4v2.title: Restricted project can use pull mode migration through clustered refresh
GHSA-443p-7392-h4v2.description: ### Summary Restricted projects aren't allowed to use pull mode migration, as that has the server connect to an arbitrary remote URL chosen by the user. That rule is enforced by the instance creation check, but on clustered servers a migration request with `refresh` set for an instance that already exists locally takes a short-circuit straight into the migration sink and never runs that check. ### Impact A user with instance creation rights in a restricted project on a clustered server can have the server open an outbound TLS websocket connection to a URL of their choice, trusting a certificate they supply. This can be used to probe services reachable from the server. The refresh only synchronizes storage for an instance the user already owns, so no configuration bypass results from it. Standalone servers are not affected. ### Details The pull mode restriction is now enforced at the start of the refresh short-circuit, before the request is forwarded to another member or the migration sink is set up. ### Workarounds Don't grant instance creation in restricted projects on clustered servers to users who shouldn't be able to initiate outbound connections from the server.

GHSA-hpjh-q53p-f27r.title: Arbitrary file write on host via path traversal in instance backup dependent volumes
GHSA-hpjh-q53p-f27r.description: ### Summary Importing an instance backup validates the instance name and snapshot names, but not the names of the dependent custom volumes listed in the backup's `index.yaml`. Those names are used verbatim as path segments when creating the volume on the target storage pool, so a `../` chain escapes the storage pool directory. ### Impact Any client allowed to create instances in a project can have the Incus daemon create root-owned directories, populated with attacker-controlled content, at arbitrary paths on the host, leading to full host compromise. The backup also names the project each dependent volume is created in, so the same request could create custom volumes in projects the caller has no access to. ### Details The fixes for CVE-2026-81495 and CVE-2026-81496 added name validation to the direct custom volume and instance backup import handlers. The dependent volume path nested inside an instance backup reaches the same volume creation code without going through either check. The name flows through `filepath.Join`, which collapses `../`, into `os.Mkdir` and the subsequent unpacking of the volume data. The attached-device gate can be satisfied by splitting the traversal string across the device's `pool` and `source` fields, as only the pool of the volume entry is resolved against a real storage pool. ### Workarounds Only allow trusted clients to create instances.

GHSA-jh4v-j34r-2mgh.title: Project restriction bypass for custom volume copy with omitted source type
GHSA-jh4v-j34r-2mgh.description: ### Summary Creating a custom storage volume with a `source` volume but no `source.type` is handled as a copy, but the source volume access check only applies when `source.type` is explicitly set to `copy`. A request that omits the type goes straight to the copy code path with a caller-controlled `source.project`. ### Impact Any client allowed to create custom volumes in a project can copy any custom volume from any other project on the server, including its snapshots and configuration, and read its contents, defeating project isolation. ### Details The `POST /1.0/storage-pools/{pool}/volumes/custom` endpoint only checks `can_create_storage_volumes` on the target project. The `can_view` check on the source volume added for CVE-2026-55621 lives in the `copy` arm of the source type switch, while the empty type arm calls the same copy helper without it. The official client always sets `source.type` to `copy`, so the empty form is only reachable through a crafted request.

GHSA-mmj7-8rgf-mx2h.title: Read of other bucket objects via unsigned header on presigned S3 upload URL
GHSA-mmj7-8rgf-mx2h.description: ### Summary The in-process S3 server used for storage buckets on local storage pools verifies SigV4 signatures over the headers listed by the client in `X-Amz-SignedHeaders`, but never checks that every `x-amz-*` header present on the request is in that list. The SigV2 presigned path doesn't include those headers in the string to sign at all. A request can therefore carry unsigned `x-amz-*` headers that change how it is handled, which AWS S3 refuses. ### Impact Anyone holding a presigned upload URL for a single object, without any bucket credentials, can add an unsigned `X-Amz-Copy-Source` header and have the server copy any other object in the same bucket onto the granted key, with the copy performed under the signer's credentials. If the holder can also read the target key, for instance through a matching presigned download URL, this discloses the contents of arbitrary objects in the bucket. The response also leaks the ETag of the source object. All storage pool drivers using the built-in S3 server are affected. Ceph radosgw buckets are not, and the bucket listener (`core.storage_buckets_address`) is disabled by default. ### Details The canonical request only iterates over the client-supplied signed header list, so headers outside that list are never seen by the signature check. The object handler routes any PUT carrying `X-Amz-Copy-Source` to the copy path based on the header alone, so a write grant becomes a read within the bucket. The same gap exists on the `Authorization` header path, and the SigV2 presigned path omits the `CanonicalizedAmzHeaders` section entirely. ### Workarounds Don't hand out presigned URLs for buckets that also hold sensitive objects, or keep the bucket listener disabled.

GHSA-wfvq-qh87-gm4j.title: Incus CLI arbitrary file write via malicious incus-agent during recursive file pull
GHSA-wfvq-qh87-gm4j.description: ### Summary `incus file pull -r` copies a directory tree out of a virtual machine over SFTP, served by `incus-agent` running inside the guest. The client trusted the agent's directory listing and `Lstat` results without accounting for the fact that a compromised agent can make them inconsistent. A malicious agent can return the same entry name twice, report it as a symlink on the first visit and as a directory or regular file on the second. The client creates the symlink on the first visit and, on the second, recurses into or writes through it, escaping the local target directory. ### Impact An attacker with root inside a virtual machine, running a modified `incus-agent`, can make an operator who runs `incus file pull -r` from that virtual machine write attacker-controlled files, or whole directory trees, to arbitrary paths on the machine running the `incus` CLI, with the operator's privileges. When run as root this allows overwriting files such as `/etc/shadow` or `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`. The operator has to run a recursive pull from the compromised virtual machine; no other interaction is needed. Containers are not affected as their file transfers are served by `forkfile` on the host rather than by an in-guest agent. ### Details `sftpRecursivePullFile` in `cmd/incus/utils_sftp.go` iterates over the entries returned by `ReadDir`, calls `Lstat` on each and creates the matching local file, directory or symlink under the target. Nothing stopped a later entry from resolving to a path that the transfer itself had just created as a symlink: `os.Mkdir`/`os.Create` follow it, so the 'directory' or 'file' lands wherever the symlink points. ### Workarounds Avoid `incus file pull -r` from untrusted virtual machines, or run it as an unprivileged user into a dedicated directory.

GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j.title: Restricted client can read storage bucket keys in the default project
GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j.description: ### Summary The storage bucket key endpoints, `GET /1.0/storage-pools/{pool}/buckets/{bucket}/keys` and `GET .../keys/{key}`, only require `can_view` on the bucket and return the S3 access key and secret key. When using the TLS authorizer, a restricted client certificate is granted read-only access to buckets in the `default` project, so that projects without `features.storage.buckets` can use them. That read-only exception therefore also hands out the bucket credentials. ### Impact A client with a restricted TLS certificate scoped to any project can read the access key and secret key of every bucket in the `default` project, then use them directly against the S3 endpoint to read, modify or delete the objects in those buckets. Only the TLS authorizer is affected. OpenFGA deployments are not. ### Details Bucket keys are credentials rather than metadata, so both key retrieval endpoints now require `can_edit` on the bucket. Listing buckets and reading bucket details remain available under `can_view`. ### Workarounds Don't keep buckets in the `default` project on servers that issue restricted client certificates, or rotate the keys of any bucket a restricted client may have read.

CVE-2025-64507.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. An issue ...
CVE-2025-64507.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. An issue in versions prior to 6.0.6 and 6.19.0 affects any Incus user in an environment where an unprivileged user may have root access to a container with an attached custom storage volume that has the `security.shifted` property set to `true` as well as access to the host as an unprivileged user. A patch for this issue is expected in versions 6.0.6 and 6.19.0. As a workaround, permissions can be manually restricted until a patched version of Incus is deployed.

CVE-2026-23953.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versi ...
CVE-2026-23953.description:
Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versions 6.20.0 and below, a user with the ability to launch a container with a custom YAML configuration (e.g a member of the ‘incus’ group) can create an environment variable containing newlines, which can be used to add additional configuration items in the container’s lxc.conf due to newline injection. This can be confirmed with a second container with /tmp mounted from the host (A privileged action for validation only). A fix is planned for versions 6.0.6
and 6.21.0, but they have not been released at the time of publication.

CVE-2026-23954.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Versions ...
CVE-2026-23954.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Versions 6.21.0 and below allow a user with the ability to launch a container with a custom image (e.g a member of the ‘incus’ group) to use directory traversal or symbolic links in the templating functionality to achieve host arbitrary file read, and host arbitrary file write. This ultimately results in arbitrary command execution on the host. When using an image with a metadata.yaml containing templates, both the source and target paths are not checked for symbolic links or directory traversal. This can also be exploited in IncusOS. A fix is planned for versions 6.0.6 and 6.21.0, but they have not been released at the time of publication.

CVE-2026-33542.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. CVE-2026-33711.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus pr ...
CVE-2026-33711.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus provides an API to retrieve VM screenshots. That API relies on the use of a temporary file for QEMU to write the screenshot to which is then picked up and sent to the user prior to deletion. As versions prior to 6.23.0 use predictable paths under /tmp for this, an attacker with local access to the system can abuse this mechanism by creating their own symlinks ahead of time. On the vast majority of Linux systems, this will result in a "Permission denied" error when requesting a screenshot. That's because the Linux kernel has a security feature designed to block such attacks, `protected_symlinks`. On the rare systems with this purposefully disabled, it's then possible to trick Incus intro truncating and altering the mode and permissions of arbitrary files on the filesystem, leading to a potential denial of service or possible local privilege escalation. Version 6.23.0 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-33743.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-33743.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 6.23.0, a specially crafted storage bucket backup can be used by an user with access to Incus' storage bucket feature to crash the Incus daemon. Repeated use of this attack can be used to keep the server offline causing a denial of service of the control plane API. This does not impact any running workload, existing containers and virtual machines will keep operating. Version 6.23.0 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-33897.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-33897.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to version 6.23.0, instance template files can be used to cause arbitrary read or writes as root on the host server. Incus allows for pongo2 templates within instances which can be used at various times in the instance lifecycle to template files inside of the instance. This particular implementation of pongo2 within Incus allowed for file read/write but with the expectation that the pongo2 chroot feature would isolate all such access to the instance's filesystem. This was allowed such that a template could theoretically read a file and then generate a new version of said file. Unfortunately the chroot isolation mechanism is entirely skipped by pongo2 leading to easy access to the entire system's filesystem with root privileges. Version 6.23.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-33945.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus in ...
CVE-2026-33945.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus instances have an option to provide credentials to systemd in the guest. For containers, this is handled through a shared directory. Prior to version 6.23.0, an attacker can set a configuration key named something like `systemd.credential.../../../../../../root/.bashrc` to cause Incus to write outside of the `credentials` directory associated with the container. This makes use of the fact that the Incus syntax for such credentials is `systemd.credential.XYZ` where `XYZ` can itself contain more periods. While it's not possible to read any data this way, it's possible to write to arbitrary files as root, enabling both privilege escalation and denial of service attacks. Version 6.23.0 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-35527.title: Incus is an open source container and virtual machine manager. In ...
CVE-2026-35527.description:
Incus is an open source container and virtual machine manager. In versions prior to 7.0.0, the image import flow issues an outbound HEAD request to a user-supplied URL before validating the request against project restrictions such as restricted.images.servers. The imgPostURLInfo function constructs and sends a HEAD request directly from the attacker-supplied source URL to resolve image metadata, and this network interaction occurs before the flow reaches the point where the import would be rejected by policy. Although the actual image download is blocked by the project restriction, an authenticated user can coerce the daemon into making blind HEAD requests to arbitrary destinations.

These requests include server metadata in custom headers (Incus-Server-Architectures, Incus-Server-Version), which discloses information about the host environment to the attacker-controlled endpoint. This blind SSRF primitive can be used to probe internal services, unroutable address space, or cloud metadata endpoints reachable from the host.

This vulnerability pattern is similar to CVE-2026-24767. This issue has been fixed in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-40243.description:
Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versions before 7.0.0, broken TLS validation logic in the OVN database connection logic can allow connections to an attacker's OVN database. The OVN client implementations disable Go standard TLS server verification and replace it with custom peer-certificate verification logic. CVE-2026-81496.title: Arbitrary file write on host via path traversal in instance backup import
CVE-2026-81496.description: ## Summary `POST /1.0/instances` with an `application/octet-stream` body (instance backup import) reads the instance name from the tarball's `backup/index.yaml` verbatim and uses it as an on-disk path segment. A project user with the `can_create_instances` entitlement can set `name: ../../../../etc/cron.d/x`, causing the root Incus daemon to create a directory and unpack attacker-controlled tarball content outside the storage pool - before any name validation runs. This yields arbitrary directory creation and arbitrary-content file write as root, and thus host RCE. ## Root Cause In `createFromBackup` (`cmd/incusd/instances_post.go`), the tarball metadata is parsed by `backup.GetInfo` (`internal/server/backup/backup_info.go:64-160`), which loads `result.Name` straight from `index.yaml` via YAML unmarshal with NO validation - no `filepath.Clean`, no `IsAPIName`, no `/` or `..` rejection. The name then flows to `pool.CreateInstanceFromBackup` -> `project.Instance(srcBackup.Project, srcBackup.Name)` (`internal/server/storage/backend.go:744`) -> `vol.MountPath()` -> `GetVolumeMountPath` = `VarPath('storage-pools', pool, 'containers', <name>)` -> `EnsureMountPath` `os.Mkdir` + `CreateVolumeFromBackup` content unpack. `instance.ValidName` exists only at `instances_post.go:1452`, which is on the JSON-dispatch path and is never reached for the octet-stream branch (dispatch returns at `:1157`). ## Impact Root-owned arbitrary directory creation and arbitrary-content file write outside the storage pool (e.g. `/etc/cron.d/`), leading to host remote code execution. Snapshot names (`bInfo.Snapshots[]`) are a second identical vector. ## Proof of Concept 1. Build an instance backup tarball whose `backup/index.yaml` sets `name: ../../../../etc/cron.d/pwn` and whose `container/rootfs` contains a crafted cron file body. 2. `curl -X POST --data-binary @backup.tar -H 'Content-Type: application/octet-stream' https://incus/1.0/instances` (as a user with `can_create_instances`). 3. The daemon writes attacker content to `/etc/cron.d/pwn` as root. ## Attack Chain 1. Entry: `POST /1.0/instances`, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, no `X-Incus-name`. Guard: none for this branch -> `createFromBackup` (`instances_post.go:1157`). 2. Parse: `bInfo, _ := backup.GetInfo(backupFile, ...)` (`instances_post.go:851`) reads `Name` from `index.yaml`. Guard: `GetInfo` (`backup_info.go:64-160`) - none. Bypass proof: field returned untouched from YAML unmarshal; no `Clean`/`IsAPIName`/`..` check in the function (verified at HEAD). 3. Restriction check: `AllowInstanceCreation` (`instances_post.go:871`) validates project restrictions only, not name syntax. Passes. 4. Sink: `pool.CreateInstanceFromBackup(*bInfo, ...)` (`instances_post.go:992`) -> `project.Instance(proj, bInfo.Name)` (`backend.go:744`) -> `vol.MountPath()` -> `EnsureMountPath` `os.Mkdir` (`internal/server/storage/drivers/volume.go`) + content unpack, as root, BEFORE `internalImportFromBackup` and BEFORE the unreachable `ValidName` at `:1452`. 5. Impact: root arbitrary dir create + attacker-content file write -> host RCE. ## Bypass Evidence No guard exists between the tarball name and the disk write. Go's `filepath.Join` collapses `..`: `filepath.Join('/var/lib/incus/storage-pools/p/containers','../../../../etc/cron.d/x')` = `/var/lib/etc/cron.d/x` (verified by running it; deeper `..` reaches `/etc/cron.d/x`). Same class as CVE-2026-48753 but a distinct, unfixed entry point (record name used as path segment, not a symlink inside the archive payload). ## Affected Versions `<= 7.2.0` (vulnerable code verified present on latest release tag v7.2.0 and on HEAD 60d85b3e; no fix commit on `cmd/incusd/instances_post.go` between v7.2.0 and HEAD). ## Suggested Fix Apply `instance.ValidName(bInfo.Name, false)` (and validate each snapshot name) immediately after `backup.GetInfo`, before any storage I/O. ## Credit Vulnerability independently discovered and responsibly disclosed by Zhixi 'Jace' Sun (@manus-use).

CVE-2026-81501.title: Restricted client can import a private image from another project
CVE-2026-81501.description: ### Summary A project-restricted TLS client that cannot `GET /1.0/images/{fingerprint}` for a **private** image in another project can still import that same fingerprint into their own project. `imageDownload` reuses any matching local image via `GetImageFromAnyProject` without checking `Public` or `CanView`. Image blobs are stored globally under `var/images/<fingerprint>`, so the caller receives the private image properties and files. This is the image-object counterpart of GHSA-c9f5-j9c3-mhrg (instance copy from `req.Source.Project` without `CanView`). It is not a privileged-container escape. ### Affected - Runtime reproduction: Ubuntu 24.04 package **Incus 6.0.0** (`6.0.0-1ubuntu0.3`) in an isolated Docker environment. - Same unguarded call is present on `lxc/incus` at `v7.3.0-432-gf216a6d46` in `cmd/incusd/daemon_images.go`. - Full release range should be confirmed by maintainers. ### Contrast (same restricted client, same fingerprint) | Request | Result | | --- | --- | | `GET /1.0/images/<fp>?project=default` | **404** (`imageGet` requires `CanView` or public/secret) | | `POST /1.0/images?project=hunt-b` with `source.type=image` pulling from an attacker HTTPS server that only echoes `<fp>` | operation **Success**; image now listed in `hunt-b` with the victim `properties` | The attacker server never supplies image bytes. Incus clones the local private record and files. A harmless marker (`INCUS-HUNT-MARKER`) in the victim image properties appears in the attacker project. ### Impact A restricted client with `CanCreateImages` (or the ability to create an instance from an image) in their own project, who already knows a private image fingerprint from another project, can: - copy that image's properties and global blob into their project; - then view, export, or launch instances from it inside their project. This breaks Incus project isolation for private images. **Limitation:** the 64-hex fingerprint is not returned by `GET` / list to a caller without `CanView`. The attacker must obtain it out of band (logs, backups, a former project membership, a predictable custom image, etc.). No victim interaction is required after that. ### Root cause `imageGet` / `imagesGet` / `imageExport` apply `CheckPermission(ObjectImage, CanView)` and hide private images behind 404. `imageDownload`, after a dest-project miss, does: ```go _, imgInfo, err = tx.GetImageFromAnyProject(ctx, fp) // then CreateImage into the caller project — no Public / CanView check ``` Reachable from: - `POST /1.0/images` with `source.type=image` - `POST /1.0/instances` when `source.server != ''` `AllowImageDownload` only enforces `restricted.images.servers` (remote host allowlist). It is not an object-level `CanView` check. ### Suggested fix After `GetImageFromAnyProject` succeeds, only reuse the local image if: 1. `imgInfo.Public` is true, or 2. `CheckPermission` on `ObjectImage(imgInfo.Project, fingerprint)` with `EntitlementCanView` succeeds. Otherwise continue with a real remote download. Do not copy the private local image. ### Dedup Not a duplicate of: - GHSA-mq9x-prm8-3vpw / GHSA-c9f5-j9c3-mhrg — instance copy `Source.Project` without `CanView` (same class, different object and entry point) - GHSA-p8mm-23gg-jc9r — simplestreams concatenated fingerprint - GHSA-f6m5-xw2g-xc4x / GHSA-p2v3-6wvc-cv3p — fingerprint used as a filesystem path - GHSA-8gw4-p4wq-4hcv — URL import HEAD SSRF - Incus 7.3 leftover name-as-path / OpenRoot issues ### PoC Isolated Docker environment attached as `incus-private-image-anyproject.zip`. ```bash unzip incus-private-image-anyproject.zip cd incus-private-image-anyproject ./run.sh ``` Expected: `all_checks_passed: true`, `verdict=private_image_cross_project_reuse_reproduced_at_runtime`. The container starts Ubuntu 24.04 + distro Incus 6.0.0, creates a private image in `default` (marker in `properties.description`), a project `hunt-b`, and a restricted TLS cert bound only to `hunt-b`. It then runs the contrast above. Harmless marker only; no instance is launched. `results/runtime.json` from our run is included. ### Severity Medium. Suggested: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` = 6.3. | Metric | Value | Reason | | --- | --- | --- | | AV | N | HTTPS API | | AC | H | 64-hex fingerprint required; not enumerable via GET/list (404) | | PR | L | project-restricted TLS client with image-create rights, not admin | | UI | N | no victim interaction | | S | C | breaks project isolation (same Scope as GHSA-c9f5) | | C | H | full private image (properties + rootfs blob) | | I | N | victim image is not modified | | A | N | no availability impact | If maintainers treat fingerprint knowledge like instance-name knowledge in GHSA-c9f5, the matching vector is `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` = 7.7. I am reporting 6.3. ### Credit Yuliang Xiao

GHSA-443p-7392-h4v2.title: Restricted project can use pull mode migration through clustered refresh
GHSA-443p-7392-h4v2.description: ### Summary Restricted projects aren't allowed to use pull mode migration, as that has the server connect to an arbitrary remote URL chosen by the user. That rule is enforced by the instance creation check, but on clustered servers a migration request with `refresh` set for an instance that already exists locally takes a short-circuit straight into the migration sink and never runs that check. ### Impact A user with instance creation rights in a restricted project on a clustered server can have the server open an outbound TLS websocket connection to a URL of their choice, trusting a certificate they supply. This can be used to probe services reachable from the server. The refresh only synchronizes storage for an instance the user already owns, so no configuration bypass results from it. Standalone servers are not affected. ### Details The pull mode restriction is now enforced at the start of the refresh short-circuit, before the request is forwarded to another member or the migration sink is set up. ### Workarounds Don't grant instance creation in restricted projects on clustered servers to users who shouldn't be able to initiate outbound connections from the server.

GHSA-hpjh-q53p-f27r.title: Arbitrary file write on host via path traversal in instance backup dependent volumes
GHSA-hpjh-q53p-f27r.description: ### Summary Importing an instance backup validates the instance name and snapshot names, but not the names of the dependent custom volumes listed in the backup's `index.yaml`. Those names are used verbatim as path segments when creating the volume on the target storage pool, so a `../` chain escapes the storage pool directory. ### Impact Any client allowed to create instances in a project can have the Incus daemon create root-owned directories, populated with attacker-controlled content, at arbitrary paths on the host, leading to full host compromise. The backup also names the project each dependent volume is created in, so the same request could create custom volumes in projects the caller has no access to. ### Details The fixes for CVE-2026-81495 and CVE-2026-81496 added name validation to the direct custom volume and instance backup import handlers. The dependent volume path nested inside an instance backup reaches the same volume creation code without going through either check. The name flows through `filepath.Join`, which collapses `../`, into `os.Mkdir` and the subsequent unpacking of the volume data. The attached-device gate can be satisfied by splitting the traversal string across the device's `pool` and `source` fields, as only the pool of the volume entry is resolved against a real storage pool. ### Workarounds Only allow trusted clients to create instances.

GHSA-jh4v-j34r-2mgh.title: Project restriction bypass for custom volume copy with omitted source type
GHSA-jh4v-j34r-2mgh.description: ### Summary Creating a custom storage volume with a `source` volume but no `source.type` is handled as a copy, but the source volume access check only applies when `source.type` is explicitly set to `copy`. A request that omits the type goes straight to the copy code path with a caller-controlled `source.project`. ### Impact Any client allowed to create custom volumes in a project can copy any custom volume from any other project on the server, including its snapshots and configuration, and read its contents, defeating project isolation. ### Details The `POST /1.0/storage-pools/{pool}/volumes/custom` endpoint only checks `can_create_storage_volumes` on the target project. The `can_view` check on the source volume added for CVE-2026-55621 lives in the `copy` arm of the source type switch, while the empty type arm calls the same copy helper without it. The official client always sets `source.type` to `copy`, so the empty form is only reachable through a crafted request.

GHSA-mmj7-8rgf-mx2h.title: Read of other bucket objects via unsigned header on presigned S3 upload URL
GHSA-mmj7-8rgf-mx2h.description: ### Summary The in-process S3 server used for storage buckets on local storage pools verifies SigV4 signatures over the headers listed by the client in `X-Amz-SignedHeaders`, but never checks that every `x-amz-*` header present on the request is in that list. The SigV2 presigned path doesn't include those headers in the string to sign at all. A request can therefore carry unsigned `x-amz-*` headers that change how it is handled, which AWS S3 refuses. ### Impact Anyone holding a presigned upload URL for a single object, without any bucket credentials, can add an unsigned `X-Amz-Copy-Source` header and have the server copy any other object in the same bucket onto the granted key, with the copy performed under the signer's credentials. If the holder can also read the target key, for instance through a matching presigned download URL, this discloses the contents of arbitrary objects in the bucket. The response also leaks the ETag of the source object. All storage pool drivers using the built-in S3 server are affected. Ceph radosgw buckets are not, and the bucket listener (`core.storage_buckets_address`) is disabled by default. ### Details The canonical request only iterates over the client-supplied signed header list, so headers outside that list are never seen by the signature check. The object handler routes any PUT carrying `X-Amz-Copy-Source` to the copy path based on the header alone, so a write grant becomes a read within the bucket. The same gap exists on the `Authorization` header path, and the SigV2 presigned path omits the `CanonicalizedAmzHeaders` section entirely. ### Workarounds Don't hand out presigned URLs for buckets that also hold sensitive objects, or keep the bucket listener disabled.

GHSA-wfvq-qh87-gm4j.title: Incus CLI arbitrary file write via malicious incus-agent during recursive file pull
GHSA-wfvq-qh87-gm4j.description: ### Summary `incus file pull -r` copies a directory tree out of a virtual machine over SFTP, served by `incus-agent` running inside the guest. The client trusted the agent's directory listing and `Lstat` results without accounting for the fact that a compromised agent can make them inconsistent. A malicious agent can return the same entry name twice, report it as a symlink on the first visit and as a directory or regular file on the second. The client creates the symlink on the first visit and, on the second, recurses into or writes through it, escaping the local target directory. ### Impact An attacker with root inside a virtual machine, running a modified `incus-agent`, can make an operator who runs `incus file pull -r` from that virtual machine write attacker-controlled files, or whole directory trees, to arbitrary paths on the machine running the `incus` CLI, with the operator's privileges. When run as root this allows overwriting files such as `/etc/shadow` or `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`. The operator has to run a recursive pull from the compromised virtual machine; no other interaction is needed. Containers are not affected as their file transfers are served by `forkfile` on the host rather than by an in-guest agent. ### Details `sftpRecursivePullFile` in `cmd/incus/utils_sftp.go` iterates over the entries returned by `ReadDir`, calls `Lstat` on each and creates the matching local file, directory or symlink under the target. Nothing stopped a later entry from resolving to a path that the transfer itself had just created as a symlink: `os.Mkdir`/`os.Create` follow it, so the 'directory' or 'file' lands wherever the symlink points. ### Workarounds Avoid `incus file pull -r` from untrusted virtual machines, or run it as an unprivileged user into a dedicated directory.

GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j.title: Restricted client can read storage bucket keys in the default project
GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j.description: ### Summary The storage bucket key endpoints, `GET /1.0/storage-pools/{pool}/buckets/{bucket}/keys` and `GET .../keys/{key}`, only require `can_view` on the bucket and return the S3 access key and secret key. When using the TLS authorizer, a restricted client certificate is granted read-only access to buckets in the `default` project, so that projects without `features.storage.buckets` can use them. That read-only exception therefore also hands out the bucket credentials. ### Impact A client with a restricted TLS certificate scoped to any project can read the access key and secret key of every bucket in the `default` project, then use them directly against the S3 endpoint to read, modify or delete the objects in those buckets. Only the TLS authorizer is affected. OpenFGA deployments are not. ### Details Bucket keys are credentials rather than metadata, so both key retrieval endpoints now require `can_edit` on the bucket. Listing buckets and reading bucket details remain available under `can_view`. ### Workarounds Don't keep buckets in the `default` project on servers that issue restricted client certificates, or rotate the keys of any bucket a restricted client may have read.
